questions.stem: Amylase is found in saliva and is also produced by the pancreas. It breaks down starch into maltose. When food enters the stomach, salivary amylase stops working. Why?

options.text: The stomach has no starch present
The low pH (acidic conditions) in the stomach denatures the amylase
Pepsin destroys the amylase
Amylase only works in the mouth

questions.explanation: Salivary amylase has an optimum pH of about 7 (neutral). In the stomach, the pH drops to 1-2 due to hydrochloric acid. This extreme change in pH denatures the amylase, changing its active site shape so it can no longer bind to starch. Starch digestion resumes in the duodenum when pancreatic amylase is added.

questions.stem: Lipase breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. Bile is also needed for efficient fat digestion. What role does bile play?

options.text: Bile is an enzyme that digests fats
Bile emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase to work on
Bile provides the acidic pH lipase needs
Bile absorbs the fatty acids directly

questions.explanation: Bile is NOT an enzyme -- it does not chemically break down fats. Instead, bile salts emulsify large fat globules into many tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area available for lipase enzymes to act upon. This dramatically speeds up fat digestion. Without bile, fat digestion would be extremely slow.

questions.stem: A student adds protease enzyme to a solution of egg white (protein) in a test tube at 37 degrees C. After 30 minutes, the cloudy solution becomes clear. What does this observation indicate?

options.text: The egg white has evaporated
The insoluble protein has been digested into soluble amino acids
The protease has been denatured
The temperature was too high

questions.explanation: Egg white is cloudy because it contains insoluble protein (albumin). When protease enzymes break down the protein into amino acids, these are soluble and form a clear solution. The clearing of the solution indicates that digestion has occurred. This is a standard practical for investigating protease activity.

questions.stem:
The table shows where different digestive enzymes work:
- Mouth: amylase (pH 7)
- Stomach: pepsin (pH 2)
- Small intestine: trypsin, lipase, amylase (pH 8)

Why do different parts of the digestive system have different pH levels?

options.text: Random variation with no biological purpose
Each region's pH matches the optimum pH of the enzymes that work there
Acidic conditions are needed everywhere but only the stomach can produce acid
pH does not affect enzyme function

questions.explanation: Different enzymes have different optimum pH values due to their specific protein structures. The digestive system creates the appropriate pH in each region: neutral saliva in the mouth for amylase, acidic conditions in the stomach for pepsin, and alkaline conditions in the small intestine (aided by bile) for trypsin, lipase, and pancreatic amylase.

questions.stem: After digestion, starch has been broken down to maltose and then to glucose. Protein has been broken down to amino acids. Fats have been broken down to fatty acids and glycerol. Which of these products are absorbed differently from the others?

options.text: Glucose is absorbed into lymph vessels, while amino acids go into blood
Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals (lymph vessels), while glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries
All products are absorbed into blood capillaries in the same way
Amino acids are absorbed into lacteals, while sugars and fats enter blood

questions.explanation: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into blood capillaries in the villi and travel via the hepatic portal vein to the liver. Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals (tiny lymph vessels in the villi) because they are too large to enter blood capillaries directly. They eventually enter the blood via the lymphatic system.
